title: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
summary: Build concurrent containers from CAS instead of locks: the Treiber stack, the ABA problem and tagged pointers, the Michael-Scott queue with helping, Vyukov's bounded ring, and safe memory reclamation.
outcomes: Explain what lock-free guarantees (and does not) and why a stalled lock holder blocks everyone
Trace Treiber push and pop, and pick the acquire and release orders that make them correct
Construct an ABA interleaving and fix it with counted pointers or safe reclamation
Explain how the Michael-Scott queue uses a dummy node and helping to stay lock-free
Compute Vyukov ring sequence numbers and explain why a stalled producer blocks consumers

lessons.title: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone

blocks.md:
In the memory-ordering course you used atomics with acquire and release to publish data between threads. The simplest way to share a stack or queue is still a mutex: take the lock, change the structure, release it. That works, but it has one ugly failure mode.

If the thread holding the lock is **preempted** (the OS scheduler takes its core away), takes a page fault, or simply runs slowly, every other thread that wants the structure waits. Michael and Scott list exactly these sources of delay (scheduler preemption, page faults, cache misses) as the reason blocking algorithms degrade on multiprogrammed machines.

blocks.title: Three threads, one stalled: lock versus lock-free

scenes.caption: With a lock: T1 takes the lock and is preempted at tick 1. T2 and T3 can do nothing until T1 runs again and unlocks at tick 10. Zero operations complete during the stall. (Illustrative schedule, 1 tick per operation.)

Lock-free: T1 is preempted in the middle of its operation, but it holds nothing. T2 and T3 keep completing operations, 8 of them by tick 9. When T1 wakes up, its CAS fails because the structure changed, and it simply retries.

blocks.md:
**Lock-free** is a progress guarantee, not an implementation style. Michael and Scott define a non-blocking algorithm as one that guarantees: if one or more active processes are trying to operate on the structure, *some* operation completes within a finite number of steps. Michael's hazard-pointer paper phrases it the same way: whenever a thread takes a finite number of steps, some thread (possibly a different one) has made progress.

Two neighbours on the progress ladder:

- **Blocking**: a delayed thread can stop everyone (any lock).
- **Wait-free**: *every* active thread finishes within a bounded number of its own steps, not just some thread. Lock-free allows an individual thread to starve while others keep winning.

"No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of his own bounded queue (lesson 5).

The tool that makes lock-free structures possible is **compare-and-swap (CAS)**, introduced on the IBM System/370. CAS takes an address, an *expected* value and a *new* value. Atomically, if the location still holds the expected value it is set to the new value and CAS returns true; otherwise nothing is written and it returns false.

In C++ this is `compare_exchange_weak` / `compare_exchange_strong`. On failure they also write the value actually found back into `expected`, so the retry loop does not need a separate reload. The *weak* form may fail spuriously (report false even though the values matched), for example on machines that build CAS from load-linked / store-conditional, so it belongs inside a loop.

blocks.caption: Every algorithm in this course is a variation of this loop. A failed CAS means another thread's CAS succeeded, which is exactly why the system as a whole makes progress.

blocks.prompt: Simplified model: 8 threads each want to push one item and all start at the same instant. In every round, each remaining thread reads `top` and tries its CAS; exactly one CAS wins. How many CAS attempts happen in total before all 8 pushes are done?
blocks.reveal: **36.** Round 1 has 8 attempts, round 2 has 7, and so on down to 1: $8+7+\dots+1 = 36$. That is 4.5 attempts per completed push. In general $N(N+1)/2$ attempts for $N$ pushes. Lock-free guarantees progress, not efficiency: under heavy contention most CASes fail, and each failure costs a cache-line transfer.

blocks.title: CAS attempts per completed operation (lockstep model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: everyone retries immediately and exactly one CAS per round wins. Wasted attempts grow linearly with the number of contenders.
At 32 contenders it takes 16.5 attempts per success. Real systems add backoff (Michael and Scott used bounded exponential backoff) or spread contention over many locations.

blocks.md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

blocks.question: A queue uses only atomic fetch-add and CAS, no mutex. If a producer is preempted between two of its steps, consumers can never dequeue anything past its slot until it resumes. Is the queue lock-free?
options: Yes, because it uses no locks
Yes, because consumers still return (they report empty)
No, because one stalled thread can prevent all other threads from making progress
No, because fetch-add is not a CAS
blocks.explain: The definition is about progress: some operation must complete in finite steps no matter which threads stall. Returning "empty" while items are stuck behind a stalled producer is not progress on the queue's contents. Using atomics instead of mutexes is irrelevant to the definition.

blocks.question: Why should `compare_exchange_weak` be used inside a loop?
options: It may fail spuriously even when the value matched, so the caller must be ready to retry
It is slower than the strong version and loops hide the cost
It never updates `expected`, so the loop must reload
It only works on x86
blocks.explain: cppreference: the weak form may act as if the comparison failed even when it succeeded, for example when a store-conditional loses its reservation. Inside a retry loop that is harmless, and on LL/SC machines it can be faster. It does update `expected` on failure.

lessons.title: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer

blocks.md:
The oldest and simplest lock-free structure is a stack built as a singly linked list with one shared pointer, `top`. Michael and Scott credit it to R. K. Treiber (IBM research report RJ 5118, 1986), and Michael's hazard-pointer paper traces the same free-list algorithm back to the IBM System/370 documentation. Michael and Scott use it as the lock-free free list for their queue nodes.

The whole state of the stack is one word, so one CAS on that word can push or pop atomically.

blocks.caption: Treiber stack in C++. Correct only if popped nodes are never freed or reused while another thread might still be inside pop (lesson 3 and lesson 6).

blocks.title: Push under contention: the CAS catches a lost race

scenes.caption: T1 wants to push node X onto a stack whose top is A. It reads top into the private variable old.
T1 links X in front of what it saw. X is still private, so this plain store races with nobody.
Meanwhile T2 pushes B, so top is now B. T1's CAS compares top (B) with old (A): mismatch, nothing is written, and old is refreshed to B.
scenes.output: CAS failed: top changed from A to B

scenes.caption: Back to the loop body: X.next is re-pointed at B, the top T1 now believes in.
This time top still equals old, so the CAS installs X. The successful CAS is the instant the push takes effect.

blocks.md:
A concurrent structure is **linearizable** if every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its call and its return (Herlihy and Wing's definition, as quoted by Michael and Scott). That point is the **linearization point**. For the Treiber stack it is the successful CAS on `top`, for both push and pop. Failed CASes change nothing, so they cannot be observed.

For pop, an empty stack is observed at the load that returns null.

**Why these memory orders.** Push writes `n->value` and `n->next` with plain stores, then publishes `n` with the CAS. Making the successful CAS a *release* and pop's loads of `top` *acquire* creates the happens-before edge from the prerequisite course: a thread that pops `n` is guaranteed to see the fields written before it was pushed.

Pop needs acquire on the failure path too, because a failed CAS reloads `old` and the very next thing pop does is read `old->next`, which another thread wrote before publishing that node.

Pop reads `old->next` after loading `old` but before its CAS. If another thread pops `old` and frees it in that gap, the read touches freed memory. Worse, if the node is reused before the CAS, the CAS can still succeed with a stale `next`. That is the ABA problem, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.question: In `push`, T1's CAS fails. What does that tell T1?
options: Its node was lost and must be reallocated
Another thread's CAS on top succeeded since T1 read it, so the system made progress and T1 should relink and retry
The stack is full
A spurious failure always, because compare_exchange_weak never fails otherwise
blocks.explain: In this algorithm, top only changes through a successful CAS. If T1's CAS fails (ignoring rare spurious failures), some other push or pop completed. That is the lock-free argument in one sentence. T1's node is still private and simply gets relinked.

blocks.question: A colleague changes push's successful CAS to `memory_order_relaxed` to "save a fence". What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, CAS is always sequentially consistent on every CPU
Two pushes can both succeed on the same top
A popping thread may see the new node pointer but stale or uninitialized value and next fields
Pop will spin forever
blocks.explain: Atomicity of the CAS is unaffected, so two pushes cannot both win. What is lost is ordering: without release (paired with pop's acquire), the plain stores to n->value and n->next are not guaranteed visible to the thread that pops n. Some CPUs happen to be strongly ordered, but the C++ model allows the bug and compilers may reorder too.

lessons.title: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong

blocks.md:
CAS answers one question: *does this word hold the same bits I read earlier?* It cannot answer the question we actually care about: *has anything changed since I read it?*

Michael's hazard-pointer paper defines the **ABA problem**: a thread reads value A from a shared location, other threads change it to B and then back to A, and the first thread's CAS then succeeds as if nothing happened. He notes it was first reported in the documentation of CAS on the IBM System/370 and that it affects almost all lock-free algorithms. Pointers are the classic victims, because a freed node's memory is often handed straight back by the allocator.

blocks.prompt: Stack is A, B, C (A on top). T1 starts a pop: it reads old = A and next = A.next = B, then stalls. T2 pops A, pops B (and frees B), then pushes A back. T1 wakes and runs `CAS(top, A, B)`. What happens?
blocks.reveal: The CAS **succeeds**, because top holds A again. T1 sets top to B, a node that has been freed. Node C, which was really the second element, is no longer reachable: it is leaked, and the next pop reads freed memory. Nothing in T1's check could tell it that the A it sees now is a different stack state from the A it read.

blocks.title: ABA in a Treiber stack pop

nodes.label:
T1 locals:
old = A, next = B

scenes.caption: Start: top points to A, and the list is A, B, C.
T1 begins pop: it reads old = A and next = B into private variables, then is preempted before its CAS.
T2 pops A: CAS(top, A, B) succeeds. A is off the stack, but T1 still holds a pointer to it.
T2 pops B and frees it: top now points to C. T1's saved next (B) now refers to freed memory.
T2 pushes A again (the same node, or a new node the allocator placed at A's old address). The stack is A, C. Its top word holds the same bits it held at the start.
T1 wakes: CAS(top, A, B) compares top with A, they match, so top becomes B. The stack now starts at freed memory and C is lost. The CAS was right about the bits and wrong about the state.

blocks.md:
**Fix 1: counted (tagged) pointers.** Michael and Scott describe the most common solution: pair the pointer with a **modification counter**, read both together, and increment the counter on every successful CAS. A CAS that expects (A, 0) now fails against (A, 3).

The catch is width. Pointer and counter must change in one atomic step, so you need either a **double-word CAS** (CAS on two adjacent machine words) or nodes addressed by array *indices* that are small enough to share one word with the counter. Michael and Scott's queue uses exactly this `<ptr, count>` pair.

blocks.title: The same interleaving with a tag next to the pointer

scenes.caption: top holds (pointer A, tag 0). T1 reads the pair and remembers next = B, then stalls.
T2 pops A: the CAS writes (B, 1). Every successful CAS bumps the tag.
T2 pops B: (C, 2). Then T2 pushes A back: (A, 3). The pointer matches T1's again, the tag does not.
T1's CAS expects (A, 0) and finds (A, 3): it fails, reloads (A, 3), reads next = C, and its retry writes (C, 4). The stack is correct.

blocks.md: Michael and Scott are careful to say counters make ABA "extremely unlikely", not impossible: a counter of $b$ bits wraps around after $2^b$ successful CASes. If a stalled thread sleeps through exactly a multiple of that, and sees the same pointer, the bug is back.

blocks.caption: Time for a b-bit tag to wrap at an assumed rate of ten million successful CASes per second on one location. A 16-bit tag gives a stalled thread only milliseconds of safety.

blocks.md: Garbage collection does not make ABA go away in general. Michael points out that if a program moves the same node back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a stale CAS can still succeed even with perfect GC. What GC (and the schemes in lesson 6) do prevent is the special case where ABA comes from *freeing and reusing* a node someone still references.

**Fix 2: never reuse a node while anyone may still hold a reference to it.** If B cannot be freed while T1 holds it, and A cannot come back while T1 holds it, T1's CAS cannot be fooled by recycled memory. That is the job of safe memory reclamation (hazard pointers, epochs), which lesson 6 covers. First, we use counted pointers to build a queue.
CAS compares bits, not history. Any lock-free algorithm that frees or reuses nodes must either version its pointers or guarantee that no thread can still hold a reference to a node that gets reused.

blocks.question: Which change, on its own, prevents the ABA failure shown in the diagram?
options: Use compare_exchange_strong instead of compare_exchange_weak
Make every load and CAS seq_cst
Store a counter next to top that every successful CAS increments, and CAS the pair
Read old->next twice and check it did not change
blocks.explain: Strong versus weak only affects spurious failures, and stronger memory ordering does not change what bits the CAS compares. Re-reading next does not close the hole: the reuse can happen between the re-check and the CAS, and the re-read itself may touch freed memory. Only versioning the word (or preventing reuse) makes the stale CAS fail.

blocks.question: A team uses 64-bit node indices plus a 16-bit tag packed into a 128-bit word and CASes it with a double-word CAS. Their threads can be descheduled for seconds. What is the honest risk statement?
options: ABA is impossible with any tag
ABA becomes very unlikely but not impossible: the 16-bit tag wraps after 65,536 successful CASes on that word
ABA is only possible on ARM
The tag makes the algorithm wait-free
blocks.explain: Michael and Scott: counters make ABA extremely unlikely but do not guarantee it never happens. At high CAS rates a 16-bit tag wraps in milliseconds, so a long stall gives many chances. With a 128-bit word there is room for a much wider tag, which is the cheap fix.

lessons.title: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping

blocks.md:
A FIFO queue has two ends, so a single CAS on one word is no longer enough. An enqueue must do two things: link the new node after the last node, *and* move `Tail` to it. No ordinary CAS can update two separate words at once.

Michael and Scott's 1996 PODC paper, *Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms*, solves this with three ideas:

1. A **dummy node**: `Head` always points to a dummy, which is the first node of the list, so the list is never truly empty, which removes the special cases for empty and single-item queues (a technique they credit to Valois and, before him, Sites).
2. **Tail may lag**: `Tail` points to the last *or second to last* node.
3. **Helping**: any thread that finds `Tail` lagging advances it before continuing.

blocks.title: Two enqueues and a dequeue, step by step

scenes.caption: Empty queue: Head and Tail both point to the dummy D, whose next is NULL. Pointers carry a modification count, shown as <ptr, count>.
T1 enqueues A. Its CAS on D.next (E9) changes <NULL,0> to <A,1>. This CAS is the moment A is in the queue (the linearization point).
T1 is preempted before E17, so Tail still points at D: it lags one node behind. The queue is correct but Tail is stale.
T2 enqueues B. It reads Tail = D and D.next = A, which is not NULL, so it helps: CAS Tail from <D,0> to <A,1> (E13). T1 being asleep does not block T2.
T2 retries: Tail = A and A.next is NULL, so its E9 CAS links B. Then its E17 CAS swings Tail to <B,2>.
T1 wakes and runs its E17: CAS(Tail, <D,0>, <A,1>). Tail is <B,2>, so the CAS fails, and that is fine: someone already did the work.
A dequeue reads next = A, copies A's value out first (D12), then CASes Head from D to A (D13). A becomes the new dummy, and its value slot is no longer meaningful. The old dummy D is freed.

blocks.title: T2's enqueue of B, with helping

scenes.caption: T2 allocates B from the free list with next = <NULL,0>. The node is private.
It reads Tail and then Tail's next. Tail points at D, but D.next is A: Tail is lagging because T1 stalled.
Re-reading Tail confirms tail and next form a consistent snapshot.
next is not NULL, so T2 helps: CAS Tail from <D,0> to <A,1>. Then it loops.
scenes.output: helped: Tail swung D to A

scenes.caption: Second pass: tail = <A,1>, and A.next is <NULL,0>.
Tail is the last node, so T2 tries to link B. The CAS succeeds: B is now in the queue.
Finally T2 tries to swing Tail to B. If this CAS failed it would not matter: the next operation would help.

blocks.caption: Dequeue, transcribed from Figure 1 of the paper (labels D2 to D19 match the paper). Head always points to the dummy; the value lives in the node after it.

blocks.md:
**Why it is correct.** The paper proves five invariants hold at all times (assuming no ABA): the list is connected, nodes are inserted only after the last node, deleted only from the front, Head points to the first node, and Tail points to some node in the list. An enqueue takes effect at the E9 CAS that links its node; a dequeue takes effect at the D13 CAS that swings Head.

**Why it is lock-free.** Every way a loop can repeat (E7 or D5 fails, E8 fails, a CAS fails) implies another thread completed an enqueue or dequeue. A thread that stalls between E9 and E17 leaves Tail lagging by one, and every other thread knows how to fix that.

Helping is the general trick for multi-step lock-free updates: leave the structure in a state that any thread can recognise as half-finished and complete on the owner's behalf. Then no thread ever needs to wait for a specific other thread.

blocks.prompt: Why does dequeue copy `next.ptr->value` at D12 *before* its CAS on Head, instead of after it succeeds?
blocks.reveal: Once the CAS succeeds, `next` becomes the new dummy and another dequeuer may immediately dequeue past it and free it (D19 frees the *old* dummy). Reading the value afterwards could read a freed or recycled node. The paper's own comment: "Read value before CAS, otherwise another dequeue might free the next node." If the CAS fails, the copied value is simply discarded.

blocks.md:
**Measured results.** On a 12-processor SGI Challenge, the paper reports that the new non-blocking queue consistently outperformed the best known alternatives, and that blocking algorithms fared much worse under multiprogramming because an inopportune preemption can block every process. The same paper also gives a **two-lock queue** (separate head and tail locks, made safe by the same dummy node) as the choice for machines without a universal primitive like CAS or LL/SC.

Note the paper's memory model: nodes come from a Treiber-stack free list and are never returned to the OS, and the `<ptr, count>` pairs need either a double-word CAS or array indices small enough to share one word with the count. Freeing nodes to the system allocator safely needs the reclamation schemes of lesson 6.

blocks.question: A thread in enqueue reads Tail = X and finds X.next is not NULL. What does the algorithm do?
options: Wait until the thread that linked X.next swings Tail
Try to CAS Tail forward to X.next, then retry its own enqueue
Link its node after X anyway
Return failure because the queue is full
blocks.explain: That is E13: Tail is lagging, so the thread helps advance it and loops. Waiting would make the algorithm blocking, and linking after X would break the list because X is not the last node.

blocks.question: Why does a dequeuer at D6 check `head.ptr == tail.ptr` and, if the queue is non-empty, advance Tail before moving Head?
options: To keep Tail from ever pointing at a dequeued node, so dequeued nodes can be safely reused
Because Head and Tail must always be equal
To save one CAS in enqueue
Because Tail must be moved under a lock
blocks.explain: The paper: the dequeue ensures Tail does not point to the dequeued node or any predecessor, which is what lets dequeued nodes be reused. Valois's earlier algorithm let Tail lag behind Head and could not safely free nodes for exactly this reason.

lessons.title: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell

blocks.md:
Linked queues allocate a node per item and must solve reclamation. If you know the maximum size up front, an array **ring buffer** avoids both. The hard part is many producers and many consumers (**MPMC**) sharing one ring.

Dmitry Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue (published on his 1024cores site) gives every cell its own atomic **sequence number**. Two counters, `enqueue_pos_` and `dequeue_pos_`, only ever increase; a position maps to a cell with `pos & mask`, which is why the capacity must be a power of two. The cell's sequence number says whose turn it is.

blocks.tex: \text{enqueue at } pos:\ \ d = seq - pos \;\begin{cases} 0 & \text{free: try CAS on enqueue\_pos}\\ <0 & \text{full}\\ >0 & \text{another producer took it: reload} \end{cases} \qquad \text{dequeue: } d = seq - (pos+1)
blocks.caption: Initially cell i has seq = i. A producer that fills position pos sets seq = pos + 1. A consumer that empties it sets seq = pos + capacity, which is exactly the position the next lap's producer will hold.
Vyukov's enqueue (dequeue mirrors it with dif = seq - (pos + 1) and stores pos + capacity). From the 1024cores page; the original also pads the two counters onto separate 64-byte cache lines.

blocks.title: Capacity 4: sequence numbers drive every decision

scenes.caption: Fresh queue: cell i has sequence i, both counters are 0. Empty cells are shown as -.
Enqueue a at pos 0: cell 0 has seq 0, so d = 0. CAS enqueue_pos 0 to 1, write a, then store seq = 1 with release.
Enqueue b, c, d the same way. Each cell's seq is now pos + 1, meaning "full, ready for the consumer of that pos". enqueue_pos is 4.
Enqueue e at pos 4: it maps to cell 0, whose seq is 1. d = 1 - 4 = -3 < 0, so the queue is full and enqueue returns false without any CAS.
Dequeue at pos 0: d = 1 - (0 + 1) = 0. CAS dequeue_pos to 1, read a, then store seq = 0 + 4 = 4: the seq that the lap-2 producer at pos 4 expects.
Enqueue e at pos 4 now sees seq 4, d = 0, and succeeds. Cell 0 becomes seq 5. The ring has wrapped once.
Two dequeues take b and c, leaving their cells at seq 5 and 6, ready for pos 5 and pos 6.
Producer P1 claims pos 5 (cell 1) with its CAS, so enqueue_pos is 6, and then is preempted before it writes data or stores seq.
Producer P2 enqueues g at pos 6 (cell 2) and completes: seq[2] = 7. P2 was not blocked by P1.
Consumers take d and e. At pos 5 they find cell 1 with seq 5: d = 5 - 6 = -1, so dequeue returns false, looking empty, even though g is committed in cell 2. Nobody can get past P1's slot.
P1 resumes, writes f and stores seq = 6. The cell is ready again.
Dequeues at pos 5 and 6 now return f and then g, in order. Both counters are 7 and the queue is empty.

blocks.prompt: While P1 was stalled, before it resumed and published f, could any amount of retrying by consumers have delivered g?
blocks.reveal: No. Consumers take positions strictly in order through `dequeue_pos_`, and position 5 belongs to P1 until it publishes. A stalled producer that has claimed a slot blocks every consumer behind it. Producers are fine (P2 finished), but the system as a whole cannot dequeue, which is why the queue is not lock-free in the formal sense.

blocks.md: Vyukov is explicit: the queue is "not lockfree in the official meaning, just implemented by means of atomic RMW operations w/o mutexes" and he classifies it as having blocking producers and consumers. It is still excellent in practice; just do not cite it as a lock-free progress guarantee.

**Why it is fast.** Vyukov states the cost is exactly one CAS per enqueue or dequeue, with no dynamic allocation, and that producers and consumers do not touch the same data while the queue is not empty. He reports about 75 cycles per operation on average in a synthetic multi-threaded benchmark on his dual-core laptop (one machine, one benchmark).

**Why relaxed is enough on the counters.** The CAS on `enqueue_pos_` only decides *who* owns a position. The data handoff goes through the cell: the producer's release store of `seq` pairs with the consumer's acquire load of `seq`, so the consumer sees `data_`. Same pattern as the prerequisite course, applied per cell. The 64-byte padding keeps the two counters off a shared cache line so producers and consumers do not ping-pong it.

**In production.** Rust's `crossbeam_queue::ArrayQueue` says in its source that it is based on Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue. It packs a *lap* number into the high bits of each index stamp, with `one_lap` set to the smallest power of two greater than the capacity, so the capacity itself need not be a power of two: capacity 4 gives one_lap = 8, capacity 100 gives 128. Its unbounded sibling `SegQueue` is a linked list of small array segments, which crossbeam documents as somewhat slower because segments must be allocated.

blocks.question: Capacity 8. A consumer at dequeue_pos 13 reads cell 13 & 7 = 5 and sees seq = 13. What does it conclude?
options: The cell holds the item for pos 13, so try the CAS
The producer for pos 13 has not published yet: from this consumer's view the queue is empty (return false)
Another consumer already took pos 13, reload
The queue is full
blocks.explain: Dequeue computes d = seq - (pos + 1) = 13 - 14 = -1 < 0, which means empty (or the producer for 13 has claimed but not finished). The cell becomes ready when the producer stores seq = 14.

blocks.question: Why must the capacity be a power of two in Vyukov's original code?
options: Because CAS only works on power-of-two addresses
So that the cell index is pos & buffer_mask_, a cheap mask that stays consistent as pos grows forever
So that sequence numbers never wrap
Because cache lines are 64 bytes
blocks.explain: The constructor asserts buffer_size is a power of two and stores buffer_size - 1 as the mask. Masking only equals pos mod capacity for powers of two. crossbeam lifts the restriction by splitting stamps into an index and a lap instead.

lessons.title: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs

blocks.md:
Every linked structure in this course removes nodes that another thread may still be reading: the Treiber pop reads `old->next`, the Michael-Scott dequeue reads `head.ptr->next`. With a lock, the remover knows nobody else is inside, so it can call `free`. Without one it cannot know, and freeing early causes use-after-free and ABA (lesson 3).

The 1996 queue sidestepped this with a free list that reuses nodes only as queue nodes and never returns memory to the system. Valois's earlier reference-counting scheme had a worse problem: Michael and Scott report that a queue holding at most 12 items ran out of a 64,000-node free list several times in ten-million-operation runs, because one delayed reader pins every node after the one it references.

**Hazard pointers** (Michael, IEEE TPDS 2004). Each thread owns a few single-writer, multi-reader shared pointers. Before dereferencing a shared node it:

1. Loads the pointer, say `top = A`.
2. Publishes it: `hp = A`.
3. Re-reads `top` and checks it is still A. If not, start over. This proves A was reachable *after* the hazard was visible.

A thread that removes a node **retires** it into a private list instead of freeing it. When the list reaches a threshold R, it **scans** every thread's hazard pointers and frees each retired node that no hazard pointer matches.

blocks.title: A protected pop racing a remover

scenes.caption: T1 loads top = A and publishes A in its hazard slot.
T1 re-reads top. It is still A, so A was in the stack after the hazard became visible: T1 may now read A->next safely.
T2 pops A and retires it. Its scan finds A in T1's hazard slot, so A stays in T2's retired list instead of being freed.
T1's own CAS now fails (top is B). It clears its hazard and retries from the top.

add.label: CAS top A to A.next fails

scenes.caption: On T2's next scan nothing points at A, so it is freed. A stalled reader can delay only the few nodes its hazard pointers name, never the whole retired list.

blocks.md: With $N$ threads and $K$ hazard pointers each there are $H = NK$ hazard pointers in total. A scan reads all $H$, then checks each of the $R$ retired nodes. At most $H$ of them can be protected, so at least $R - H$ get freed. Michael shows that choosing $R = H + \Omega(H)$ makes the amortized cost per retired node constant, and that at most $NR$ retired nodes can be waiting at once, no matter how many threads stall.

blocks.tex: N=8,\ K=2\ \Rightarrow\ H=16;\quad R=2H=32:\ \ \text{freed per scan} \ge R-H=16,\quad \text{pending} \le NR=256
blocks.caption: Worked example: 8 threads with 2 hazard pointers each (enough for a Michael-Scott queue or a list).

blocks.title: Why R must exceed H by a constant factor

scenes.caption: Simplified cost model: a scan does H + R units of work (read every hazard pointer, look up every retired node) and frees at least R - H nodes. With R barely above H, almost every scan frees almost nothing.
At R = 2H each freed node costs at most 3 units; at R = 4H about 1.67. Larger R trades memory (up to NR pending nodes) for cheaper scans.

blocks.md: **Epoch-based reclamation (EBR)**, described in Keir Fraser's Cambridge PhD thesis (submitted 2003, published as a 2004 tech report) and used by Rust's `crossbeam-epoch`, avoids per-pointer publication. A thread **pins** itself before touching the structure, recording the global epoch it saw. Removed objects go into a garbage bag tagged with the current epoch. The global epoch may advance only when every *pinned* thread is pinned in the current epoch, and crossbeam frees a bag once the global epoch is at least 2 ahead of the bag's epoch, because a pinned thread can witness at most one advancement.

blocks.title: Epochs: a stalled reader holds back all reclamation

scenes.caption: Epoch 0. T1 unlinks node X and puts it in the bag for epoch 0. T2 may still be reading X, so nothing is freed.

At t=4 every pinned thread is in epoch 0, so the epoch advances to 1; later T1 retires Y into bag 1. At t=8 all pinned threads are in epoch 1, so it advances to 2. Bag 0 is now 2 epochs old: X is freed.
Now T3 pins at epoch 1 and stalls. The epoch can reach 2 but never 3, because T3 is pinned in an older epoch. Bag 1 (Y) and every later bag pile up: one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

blocks.md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

**What ships today.** crossbeam-epoch provides `pin()`, `Atomic`, `Shared` and deferred destruction for Rust. Facebook's Folly library has a hazard pointer implementation that, according to proposal P2530 (Hazard Pointers for C++26, by Michael and co-authors), has been in heavy production use since 2017; that paper was adopted, so C++26 has a `<hazard_pointer>` header.

A practical decision guide that follows from this course:

- Known maximum size: an array ring in the Vyukov style (crossbeam `ArrayQueue`), with no allocation per item, accepting its blocking corner case.
- Unbounded MPMC FIFO: Michael-Scott or a segmented variant (crossbeam `SegQueue`), plus EBR or hazard pointers.
- LIFO free lists and work pools: Treiber stack plus tags or reclamation.
- Low contention and no preemption worries: a plain mutex is simpler and often fine.

Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

blocks.question: In the hazard pointer protocol, why must a reader re-read the shared pointer after publishing its hazard pointer?
options: To refresh the CPU cache
Because the node may have been removed and retired between the first load and the publication, and a scan that ran in between would not have seen the hazard
To implement the ABA tag
It is optional; publishing is enough
blocks.explain: Michael's condition is that the hazard pointer must have pointed to the node continuously from a time when the node was still reachable. Re-reading proves the node was still in the structure after the hazard became visible, so any later scan will see it.

blocks.question: A service uses epoch-based reclamation. One worker thread pins, then blocks on a slow network call while still pinned. What happens?
options: Nothing: EBR is lock-free
Other threads deadlock immediately
The global epoch stops advancing past one step beyond that thread's epoch, so retired memory grows without bound until it unpins
The stalled thread's reads become unsafe
blocks.explain: Advancement requires every pinned participant to be in the current epoch. The stalled thread is fine and other threads keep operating, but garbage bags can no longer age by 2 epochs, so memory grows. Keep pinned regions short and never block inside them.

blocks.question: You need a fixed-capacity MPMC queue between 16 producers and 16 consumers, and producers may be preempted. Which statement is accurate?
options: A Vyukov-style ring has one CAS per operation and no per-item allocation, but a producer preempted after claiming a slot can delay consumers behind it
A Vyukov-style ring is wait-free
Only a Michael-Scott queue can be bounded
A Treiber stack gives FIFO order if you pop twice
blocks.explain: That is the tradeoff from lesson 5 exactly: cheap and allocation-free, blocking in the corner case where a claimant stalls. If that corner case is unacceptable, use a truly lock-free design and pay for reclamation.
